title: An Anxious Season for Muslims in Texas
author: @NewYorker
content:
Mohamed Hussein, a thirty-eight-year-old manager at a health-care company in Houston, is a lifelong conservative, describing himself as a proponent of small government who often votes Republican. He moved from Cairo to Texas as a young child, and professes “tremendous faith in America.” He is also a practicing Muslim who prays daily. In June, he went to the Republican Party of Texas State Convention, in downtown Houston, joining his father, Tarek, who was serving as a delegate.

Tarek Hussein, a physical therapist, founded the local chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the nation’s largest Muslim civil-liberties organization. With thousands of people assembled in the Houston convention center, Party members made several attempts to oust Tarek and another Muslim delegate, owing to their ties with CAIR, which Governor Greg Abbott has designated as a foreign terrorist organization. At one point, the G.O.P. chair told Tarek and the other delegate to leave the caucus. “There is a Democrat convention happening in a couple of weeks,” he said from the stage. “Join them.”

Mohamed Hussein told me that he was shocked by the hostility. At the convention, the Party approved a resolution that called on the legislature to declare Sharia a “seditious, subversive competing enemy.” Sharia is a form of guidance about how Muslims should live and worship, akin to the messages of the Ten Commandments. Yet, for two decades, many G.O.P. critics have conflated it with political extremism and terrorism carried out in the name of Islam. The resolution said that advocating for Sharia should be considered a crime, with punishments that include the stripping of U.S. citizenship and deportation. Hussein recalled, “When I read this, I’m thinking, Seditious? People to be denaturalized and deported? This is utter madness.” He added, “This is the party in power adopting this resolution with the intention of leveraging the state against a community.”

Hussein decided to remain at the convention. “I don’t know of any other solution than dialogue,” he said. On the final day, he attended a session with the Judeo-Christian Caucus, reasoning that, if Christians and Jews could come together, surely the attendees would be open to Muslim voices, too. But the moderator, a former Southern Baptist minister named Rick Scarborough, warned the attendees that they would encounter Muslims who only pretended to be accommodating. “I’ll guarantee, if they get power, they’ll cut your head off as believers of Christ,” Scarborough reportedly said.

Hussein spoke up several times. “I felt I had to preface it by apologizing to people,” he recalled, “because my intention was not to impose myself on the session, but I felt compelled to tell them that you have heard a lot of lies.” He talked with Scarborough afterward: “I asked him rhetorically, not expecting his response, ‘What do you want us to do? You want us to leave?’ In a heartbeat, he said, ‘Yes.’ ” Hussein retreated to an empty seat where he could be alone, and he wept.

The targeting of Muslims by politicians is not a new phenomenon in the United States. The attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon spawned a wave of anti-Muslim harassment and hate crimes. Donald Trump, who falsely claimed for years that Barack Obama was a Muslim, first tried to restrict immigration from majority Muslim countries nearly a decade ago. But, in his second term, he has led a groundswell of unsupported claims about an insidious Islamic presence in the country. Nearly seventy representatives have joined the Sharia-Free America Caucus, in the U.S. House of Representatives. One member, the Georgia Republican Andrew Clyde, posted on X, “No more Islamic immigration. Denaturalize, deport, repeat.”

Two weeks ago, federal agents raided the home of Ilhan Omar, a Muslim member of Congress from Minnesota whom Trump has repeatedly vilified, reportedly seizing notebooks, her mobile phone, and her passport. The goal, according to the Wall Street Journal, is to find evidence to denaturalize Omar, a Somali refugee who arrived in the United States at age twelve, and deport her. Trump has called the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, a “jihadist lunatic.”

Nowhere, it seems, has the vilification been more widespread than in Texas. Ted Cruz, the G.O.P. senator who has said that he wants to be President, told the crowd at this year’s national Republican midterm gathering in Dallas that “communists and Islamists” are “coming together and sweeping over the Democrat Party . . . . They hate Christians. They hate Jews. They hate capitalism. They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.” Earlier this year, Bo French, the Republican nominee for railroad commissioner (a position that actually oversees the regulation of oil and gas, not railroads), posted on social media, “I know I won’t rest until every muslim is gone.” Governor Abbott, a Republican who is running for a fourth term, designated CAIR a foreign terrorist organization only nine days after launching his reëlection bid. (CAIR called the move a publicity stunt with “no basis in fact or law,” and filed a lawsuit, which is ongoing.)

These attacks have prompted fresh efforts to mobilize Muslim voters in Texas. Although the group likely comprises less than two per cent of the state’s population, they could make a difference in this year’s unusually close contests for Senate, governor, and multiple congressional seats. Ahmad Siddiqi, who has served as the imam at the Kingwood Islamic Center, in the northeast Houston suburbs, since 2008, told me, “I think we were afraid in the beginning, because we would get the yelling, the screaming, and all of these things. But many of us have grown out of that phase. Now we want to stand our ground.”

On a Friday in late September, Siddiqi welcomed Imran Ghani, the director of the local chapter of CAIR—the one that Tarek Hussein founded—to address the congregation about the need for Muslim citizens to vote in November. The visit was arranged by Salam Arif, a local anesthesiologist, who said that it has been difficult to inspire his fellow-Muslims. “The perception of most of the people is: ‘Red state, my vote doesn’t count,’ ” he told me.

Ghani, who is thirty-seven and was raised mostly in Houston, had been on the job for around two months when Abbott designated CAIR as a foreign terrorist organization. “What did I just sign up for?” Ghani recalled thinking. “But very quickly I realized that this is a path of all of the great civil-rights organizations in American history. Whenever a civil-rights organization is effective, it will be targeted by certain members of the political establishment.”

At the Kingwood event, as more than two hundred men and women filed into their separate prayer halls, Ghani drew on several verses in Al-Hujurat, the forty-ninth chapter of the Quran, widely interpreted as a directive for the ethical treatment of one another and a call for Muslim unity. He said that a lack of political power has made the community an easy target. He reminded his listeners of the right to religious freedom under the Constitution, and urged them to be “openly Muslim” at a time “when there is all sorts of hatred being spewed by the political élite and our children are being attacked in schools.” And he directed the attendees to the volunteer voting registrars seated at tables in the mosque.

Afterward, Mir Ali Sadat, an internal-medicine doctor, made his way to a table to confirm that he was registered. “We have to vote,” he told me as he filled out a form. “We have to make a society where everyone respects everyone, regardless of their religion, their language, their looks, their skin, their gender.”

Jida Nabulsi is the Texas director of Emgage, a nonprofit founded twenty years ago to propel civic engagement in the Islamic community. When we met, she was standing in the blinding sun in an elementary-school parking lot in the Houston suburb of Cypress, alongside nine young staffers as they prepared to knock on hundreds of doors. Nabulsi said that the group was trying to motivate people “who are unregistered or haven’t been involved at all.” In addition to canvassing, Emgage conducts sessions in mosques and other locations that focus on the rudiments of voting. Nabulsi told me that a right-wing, anti-Muslim group had recently put up a post calling her a “Sharia operative.” In her view, the term “Islamophobia” isn’t adequate for such attacks; she prefers the more plainspoken phrase “anti-Muslim hate.”

One of the door-knockers, Abdullah Younes, a seventeen-year-old university student, allowed me to tag along as he made his rounds. He drove his black pickup truck through the exit gate of an upscale subdivision and parked on a deserted street. The work, which he has been doing since July after being recruited by a relative, can feel thankless. Guided by a canvassing app that helps Emgage workers identify likely Muslim households, he was ten houses into his route and starting to sweat through his shirt before anyone opened the door. One woman waved him away. At homes where there was no answer, he left behind a flyer that read “The polls are calling. Will you answer?”

Abdullah Antepli, a Turkish-born imam and scholar who is the president of Houston’s nonsectarian Rothko Chapel, believes that the anti-Islam rhetoric will continue, not only because it attracts votes for Republicans but also because, in his view, the response from Muslims is too weak and disjointed. Many Muslims, Antepli told me, “realize the American dream individually, but that individual success doesn’t translate into a collective civic response.” One reason, he said, is “the lack of connecting tissues between various racial and ethnic Muslim communities,” which include, among other groups, recent arrivals from “socioeconomically, politically, and historically very disconnected and fragmented parts of the world.” This lack of cohesion is evident, too, in Houston’s mosques, where, he said, many who attend prayer services “come five minutes before” and leave two minutes after the services have ended.

The day after I accompanied the Emgage canvassers, more than a dozen candidates for Congress, state legislature, and local office showed up at the Clear Lake Islamic Center, southeast of Houston, to make their pitches and take questions. Republicans were invited; none appeared. The event was part of a new monthly series led by Mohammed Nasrullah, a former Boeing project manager who once served as the chairman of CAIR-Houston’s board. He is pressing Muslim citizens to vote, in particular in local races, where a few thousand votes can be the difference. “What I notice,” he said, “is every four years they wake up and vote for President, and then they go back to sleep.”

A significant motivator this year is a revised K-12 curriculum, which was approved in September by the Republican-controlled State Board of Education and which casts Muslims in negative terms. In one lesson, students will be asked to explain early Islam in terms of the Prophet Muhammad’s “brutal military campaigns against Jewish and Christian tribes, the normalization and regulation of slavery, and the taking of female captives as harem slaves.” In another, they will have to describe “the teachings of jihad and how these teachings led to the expansion of Islam and the conquest of Christian lands.”

Dana Van De Walker, who is a professor and administrator at a community college in the northern Houston suburbs and a candidate for the State Board of Education, was campaigning at a mosque for the second time in forty-eight hours. Flipping just a few of the fifteen seats on the board, she told me, would give Democrats a majority and a chance to overturn the curriculum vote. “The thing that really pisses me off as a teacher,” she said, “is that we’re spending so much time talking about Islamophobia that we can’t talk about how we’re forty-fourth in the nation in eighth-grade English language-arts/literacy scores.”

As Rabeea Sultan Collier, a district-court judge who is running for reëlection, told the Clear Lake audience, the solution is as simple as it is urgent: “This last year, we have been under attack in a way that we’ve never seen before. So we want you to come out in numbers like they’ve never seen before.” ♦

title: Portable Translators Can Help You Speak Like a Local When Traveling Abroad
author: @wired
content:
Hans Christian Andersen once said, “To travel is to live,” and while that’s a romantic notion, he probably wasn’t careening through Gyeongju, South Korea, at midnight in the back of a taxi with a driver who didn’t speak a lick of English.

A lot has changed since the 1800s, to be fair. Today’s world traveler has it awfully easy when it comes to understanding the local lingo, as even a basic modern cell phone app can offer a pretty good translation of common phrases delivered in everything from Abkhaz to Zulu. Type or speak a sentence or two into the app, tap a button, and out it returns in the language of your choice. Tap another button, and your phone can even speak those sentences aloud. It takes a little doing to turn this into a credible two-way conversation—especially if the cab driver isn’t slowing down—but with some patience and good humor, two strangers can engage in a reasonable discussion this way.

Casual travelers merely in need of directions to the farmacia or who want to know exactly what they’re getting into with a plate of kycklingtallrik can get by with a phone and a translation app, and if you’re going to a place with a fairly common tongue, you may not even need an active internet connection if you download the relevant language file for offline use. Google Translate, Apple Translate, or DeepL Translate will all do the job for free, though Google’s product is widely considered the gold standard for cross-language chitchat.

But what if you want to push past translating menus and asking for extra towels and carry on a conversation with a new friend you met on a trip or the in-laws who are visiting from halfway across the world? That’s where a handheld translator device can prove invaluable. These pocket-sized digital interpreters can help you seem like a polyglot, even if you don't know simple phrases. I have been testing and reviewing handheld translators for WIRED for five years, and I've developed a keen sense of how a good product should work and which ones I'd recommend.

What Do Handheld Language Translators Do?

Handheld translators are exactly that—stand-alone devices that up the ante on language interpretation, and their real value is revealed when you use them for sustained, voice-based conversation. Alongside the spoken word, some have a screen that shows the translation in text, often displaying the other side of the conversation upside down, so you don’t have to constantly pass the device back and forth.

Having a translator in a separate piece of hardware has further advantages. Namely, you can use your phone for something else while you’re talking—like snapping pictures or taking notes, for example—instead of tethering it to a translation app. You may also feel more comfortable handing a less costly stand-alone device to someone you don’t know versus trusting them with your $1,000 smartphone.

Many handheld translators can operate independently, either via Wi-Fi or with preloaded data plans that generally work worldwide. That means you can take one on a global jaunt and have access to interpretation services without having to pony up for an international plan on your smartphone. Better yet, download all the language packs you want before your trip, and you can use a handheld translator in offline mode, even when you’re in the sticks.

Earbud-based translators are the next game changer. These are over-ear devices that come in a pair—one for you, one for your conversation partner. Each of you wears one earbud, and the software on your phone handles the translation, both ways, behind the scenes. The best earbud translators make for the most natural way to communicate with someone in a foreign language that I’ve found to date, though handhelds tend to have more capabilities. (Earbud-based designs seem to be the direction the industry is heading.)

When shopping for a handheld translator, watch out for expensive subscription plans. Many devices come with free service, but only for a time, and re-upping after the trial period ends can be pricey. Check the fine print before you buy. Also, make sure the translator you’re considering covers all the languages you need. Note that while some translators support hundreds of languages, they may be limited in the language pairs they can translate between.

Who Really Needs a Handheld Language Translator?

Again, if you only need casual translation for occasional or emergency use, you can definitely get by with a free translation app on your phone. Translation devices are best for frequent users who expect to carry on multiple sustained conversations with speakers of other languages over time.

Those scenarios could include attending a reunion with your Swedish wife’s extended family or a lengthy workshop series with colleagues from other parts of the world. These tools are also often marketed to first responders who need to quickly assess a situation when human translation services aren’t available.

In situations where you may need to communicate with several speakers, each speaking a different language, a portable translator can make even more sense. If you expect your journeys to take you to far-flung areas or off the grid entirely, where internet service may be poor or nonexistent, a translator can be a helpful tool in your travel bag, even if you only expect to use it for emergencies.

The Best Stand-Alone Translator

  • Photograph: Chris Null

  • Photograph: Chris Null

  • Photograph: Chris Null

Timekettle

T1 Handheld Translator Device

The Timekettle T1 is a reasonably affordable and very pocketable device that makes for an easy addition to your travel kit. Built for two users to communicate, each with access to half the screen, the T1 translates each side of a conversation—written or spoken—into that user’s own language. Using it can be a little tricky: A color-coded button on the side of the device or a virtual one on the 4-inch touchscreen must be held down to tell the T1 which language to listen for. But once you get the hang of it, the system works pretty well.

Accuracy is solid, and translations are fast, popping up in well under a second. One challenge I had with the device relates to its small screen. Like most translators, the T1 supports photo-based translations via its 8-megapixel camera, but the 540 x 1080-pixel screen is too small to display much text at once. Also, while the unit includes a global eSIM with two years of free service included ($50/year after that), I encountered plenty of signal gaps, even in my own home. The good news is that if Wi-Fi’s available, that works, too. The unit also supports 31 offline language pairs (10 in combination with English), so if you plan ahead, service woes may not be an issue at all.

Best Translator Earbuds

Courtesy of iFLYTEK

iFLYTEK

iFLYTEK AI Translation Earbuds

If you want to upgrade your translation experience and make it more immersive, you’ll want to invest in a pair of earbuds, which give you a more personal and natural way to communicate. As described above, the iconic way to use these is to pop one on yourself and give the other to your friend. An app on your phone handles two-way translation, back and forth.

These 12-gram on-ear earbuds are the best I’ve tested, primarily because once they’re configured, they work completely hands-free. No clicking buttons or tapping the side of your head every time you’re ready to speak: The earbuds understand who’s talking and when, and they work with remarkable speed, almost like a professional interpreter whispering in your ear.

You can also wear both earbuds and use them for one-way translations, including phone calls. The only trouble with the setup is that there’s no offline mode, so you’ll need internet access on your phone for them to do anything.

Timekettle

W4 Plus AI Interpreter Earbuds

Another excellent choice is Timekettle’s W4 Plus AI Interpreter Earbuds. While these $379 earbuds are smaller at 6 grams each and work nearly identically to iFLYTEK’s (completely hands free), I found the form factor to be a little less stable and the bulky charging case much more awkward to tote around. The extra outlay does however get you a limited offline mode and some built-in AI tools, including a meeting summarizer.

Best AI Translator Companion Device

Photograph: Chris Null

InnAIO

T10 AI Voice Cloning Translator

The InnAIO T10 is a hybrid device that serves as both an AI notetaker and a language translator. It has no screen and only one button, and a MagSafe ring allows it to clip to the back of your phone to ensure it’s always in reach.

Like other translators, the device is designed to record, transcribe, and summarize thoughts and meetings, but it can also translate them in real time. It’s better with written translations, but it also supports audio translations, though using this feature is slightly more difficult, requiring each party to hold down a button in the mobile app every time they speak.

The T10 has been upgraded since I wrote my review, adding an offline mode and enhancing a few other features, but note that you’ll still need a subscription ($179/year for unlimited service) to make the most of it, as the free tier only supplies 120 minutes of real-time translation per month.

Best Large Group Translation System

Photograph: Christopher Null

Timekettle

X1 Meeting Interpreter Hub

The X1 Meeting Interpreter Hub works a lot like other translation systems, except it’s designed for multiple participants. The brick-like device contains two earbuds for live audio, plus a screen that displays translated spoken dialogue in real-time. If everyone in a room is outfitted with a hub–up to 10, total–each user can understand what everyone else is saying, with a maximum of 5 languages supported simultaneously. This can be further extended to remote users accessing the meeting online by sharing the meeting via a QR code that’s generated for each new discussion. Online, 60 remote participants can get live access to both text and audio translations, and contribute their own thoughts via voice by holding down a button on the web-based interface whenever they wish to speak. (There’s no app involved with the X1, no matter how you use it.)

The X1 is versatile and can also be used for one-on-one conversations (wherein each user shares an earbud) or as a simple streaming media translation/captioning device. A total of 52 languages and 106 accents are supported, and you can even change the gender of translations to match that of your conversation partner. After a meeting, the device can optionally generate AI summaries of the discussion (in your own language, naturally); these are delivered via web browser and a QR code link and expire after seven days.

The X1 is not a simple device–everything is done by tapping on its 3.4-inch touchscreen–nor is it an inexpensive one at $849. And remember, a separate unit is required for each seat in the room. You can do the math on what ten of these will cost you (or your company’s) bank account.

title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
author: Emma Roth
content:
Emma Roth

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union.

It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.”

Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future.

Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards.

It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

title: FromSoftware is temporarily shutting down online servers for Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3, and blames an unknown "server issue" for the downtime
author: Kaan Serin
content:
Tarnished.

Things might get even darker over in the world of Lordran without those silly, only sometimes helpful notes left by other players. Developer FromSoftware has announced that it's temporarily closing Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 servers because of an unspecified issue.

"Due to a server issue, the game servers for the following titles will be temporarily unavailable on all platforms," the RPG studio tweeted earlier today, before naming Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3.

While the server shutdown won't last forever, FromSoftware hasn't told series fans when exactly they can expect online play to be restored. That presumably means PvP invasions, summon signs and in-game messages that try to troll you off a cliff are unavailable for the time being.

"We will provide updates once we have information regarding the server restoration time. We apologize for the inconvenience," the studio added. I hope you've stocked up on Estus Flasks, at least.

Of course, this isn't the first time the Dark Souls trilogy has had to contend with server problems. In 2022, Bandai Namco took servers for all three Dark Souls games offline due to a security vulnerability affecting Dark Souls 3. The threequel went dark once again a few months later.

FromSoftware's next game The Duskbloods - the one with the jetpacks and vampires and a cute bird thing - hasn't been any luckier, either. The multiplayer-focused game's first network test had to be taken offline early due to similarly vague "server issues". More recently, FromSoftware delayed its Switch 2 exclusive into next year.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," the developer tweeted this week. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

title: After a year of testing, one of Steam's best features is finally out of beta, making it easier to find games you might actually like
author: Sherif Saed
content:
The Valve index.

Steam's Personal Calendar, a feature Valve has been testing for nearly a year, has finally left beta and is now available for everyone.

Personal Calendar, which initially launched as a Steam Labs experiment last October, works by highlighting upcoming games and recent releases - tailored to your interests - and arranging them by release date. The feature has its own section on the store homepage, and also has a dedicated page showing the games Steam's algorithm believes you're going to like, meaning what's included is different for everyone.

While Steam has always had several ways of recommending games to players based on their tastes, Personal Calendar takes it a step further by having a stricter recommendation criteria and arranging the results in an intuitive, month-based way that's less likely to overwhelm.

Valve says its recommendation engine relies on three key metrics: it looks at your recently played games, finds other players with similar playtime profiles, then looks at the games those players have been playing or adding to their wishlists. In a blog post, Valve explains only games "you play the most" are considered, meaning titles you try for a few minutes won't factor into your recommendations.

Crucially, the Personal Calendar's recommendations are not static, and Valve notes they're refreshed daily to incorporate new data where available. "In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day," it writes, "but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the eight-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

Incidentally, Valve is aware the feature could end up having the opposite effect, i.e., limiting the number of games a player potentially sees because they fall outside their filters, essentially trapping them inside a bubble. The developer doesn't have a clear solution for that potential problem, but says it wants to keep things varied.

"With the Personal Calendar, it's unlikely that every day has a new game launching that is the same genre/theme as games you've been playing and is also a good recommendation for you," Valve explains. "As a result, the recommendations generated by the Personal Calendar end up drawing from a wider pool of titles across all kinds of genres that are releasing each day."

title: The Middle-Aged Misanthropes of the Wisconsin Trilogy
author: @NewYorker
content:
“Every character should want something,” goes an overused adage of fiction-writing workshops, popularized by Kurt Vonnegut. (“Even if it is only a glass of water,” he added.) Novels centered on gay male experiences have, historically, epitomized this maxim. There’s the want for sex, often lots of it; for youth, exemplified most famously by Thomas Mann’s 1912 novella, “Death in Venice”; and for acceptance from straight culture, especially in work birthed during the peak of the AIDS crisis, such as “Second Son” (1988), by Robert Ferro, in which a man with a deadly virus navigates his relationship with his close-knit family. Not to mention, a desire for glamour and for life’s finer things—travel abroad and summers in the country—that must be chased the way a collector would an unpaid credit-card bill. Edmund White’s 2016 gem, “Our Young Man,” opens with portrayals of a journalist and a bartender who scrape together their incomes in order to afford a house share on the Fire Island Pines in the early nineteen-eighties—a luxury, the book implies, that would be financially prohibitive in this millennium.

The first-person speakers of Nate Lippens’s Wisconsin Trilogy have checked out from want. They toil as bartenders and caterers; off the clock, they’re misanthropes with a few trusted confidants and a bevy of deceased acquaintances who occupy their thoughts. Across Lippens’s cycle of semi-autobiographical novels—“My Dead Book,” from 2021; “Ripcord,” from 2024; and “Bastards,” on shelves this fall—these unnamed narrators share biographical details, enough that they seem to be the same character. Each fled home and school at fifteen, learning from a ragtag, self-designed syllabus of twentieth-century literature, cult cinema, punk rock, and queer art. Each endured stretches of junkiedom and stints in mental facilities, and spent young manhood hustling and hanging out with other sex workers, surviving the most disastrous period of the AIDS epidemic in the United States by becoming precociously steadfast. The narrator of “My Dead Book” recalls, about “social workers, outreach volunteers, and youth counselors” from the era, “They trained us to be vigilant. No exceptions. They saved our lives and they taught us not to trust anyone.” No surprise that he’s held on to his obstinance, as he admits elsewhere: “Negativity is my strength. I’m a man of my word and that word is usually no.”

The aging autodidacts of “Ripcord” and “Bastards” live alone in the Milwaukee area (“My Dead Book” depicts a prior spell in nearby Madison). They pass their free time watching movies, reading, remembering long talks with dead friends, chatting for hours with living ones, and wringing their hands over their chronic insomnia. They lodge their complaints in fragmented prose that splits the difference between comic zingers and poison bonbons. “Some people get the glory. Some people get the glory hole,” “Ripcord” begins. They are resigned to circumstance, their ennui wizened rather than fashionable. In “Bastards,” Lippens’s hero recounts the evening when he stopped trying:

I should make more money. That was the problem. I wasn’t succeeding. My hard work would pay off. And despite changes in names, cities, attitudes, cigarette brands, and drugs, the misbegotten notion of reward and advancement and achievement ruled until the night at the mirror. I burned my life to the ground. Job, apartment, friends, the whole goddamned thing. Afterward, clean and in shock, I saw the face in the mirror again, and I knew I wasn’t going to be a phoenix risen from my own destruction. I was going to lie in my ashes and call it done.

And he does, dispensing with professional and social ambition in a way that feels realistic. After all, most of us, queer or otherwise, make our lives in the rubble of earlier dreams of success, mobility, and, yes, liberation. Aspiring artists submit to the practical necessities of paying off debt. Vacation plans get drowned in work duties. Free spirits become shackled spouses. Lippens forges poetry from disappointment, inhabiting this mood until it becomes familiar, even a source of connection. Curmudgeons, he knows, are relatable, their lives marked by the certainty that no fantasy will ever spring them from the drudgery of survival. His survivors find dignity in the grit, a hard-fought self-love. What looks like acquiescence might actually be resilience.

“My Dead Book,” Lippens’s début novel and the first volume in the triptych, originally came out as a print-on-demand edition from the niche yet mighty press Publication Studio, in its Fellow Travelers series, an imprint dedicated to publishing overlooked writing, much of which deals in queer themes. Since then, the book, which Semiotext(e) reissued in 2024, has developed a word-of-mouth following, owing both to its coruscating prose and its frank view of twenty-first-century L.G.B.T.Q. life in the United States. The tremendous political gains that queer people made during the past two decades have given rise to a false sense of equality, concealing both the scars of history and the fresher wounds inflicted by more novel forms of homophobia. Simultaneously, as many have bemoaned in recent years, America has become too damn expensive.

Lippens’s narrators are products of this status quo. Without a college or high-school degree, their job prospects are limited. The narrator of “Ripcord” cannot pass a credit check. The narrator of “Bastards” does not have a bank account. They hook up but have given up on relationships. When a friend tries to set him up on a date, the narrator of “Ripcord,” who cannot even care for a cactus, declines: “I say I’m retired.” Blurry, half-remembered calamities have forced them to start over from nothing, again and again. The inertia of their lives weighs on them. Now, as the narrator of “My Dead Book” quips, “The only person who would say I’m young is someone else my age.”

Lippens’s début has a more straightforward—less shattered—structure than its sequels, focussing on salad days spent turning tricks and taking drugs. Its tone is elegiac, unsurprising considering that first novels so often explore the accrued pain of the writer’s life to date; still, for Lippens, that date was later than for most authors. “My Dead Book,” published when he was fifty, sports an uncommon polish and perspective for an inaugural effort. As the narrator grieves friends he lost to disease, drugs, and suicide, the book bypasses the bildungsroman to investigate more uncharted territory: the making of a crank. Childhood, he tells us, was a litany of obstacles that had to be overcome, a stretch that was “sad and confusing, and those feelings only grew with time.” The novel’s bleak, lucid tone fit the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, which was raging when the book first arrived. “Online I’ve seen friends lament their shut-in status and cabin fever, making jokes about The Shining,” its narrator reflects, comparing the isolation of an Upper Midwest winter to his own penchant for solitude. “I’m not about to tell anyone that often days, sometimes weeks, pass without me going outside.”

“Ripcord” is an arch, complex successor and in many respects a more impressive accomplishment—partly because it departs from its predecessor’s most evident influence, Gus Van Sant’s 1991 film, “My Own Private Idaho.” This Shakespearean tragedy of sex work courses through “My Dead Book” and Lippens’s plaintive evocations of the camaradarie and cavorting of hustlers in the eighties and nineties. “Ripcord” keeps us for the most part in a contemporary moment, a difficult shift that Lippens manages nimbly. He amps up the language, building an environment from his narrator’s shtick, a prosodic jungle gym of jokes, derision, self-deprecation, and asides about old Hollywood starlets, experimental writers, and outré musicians. Instead of burying bourgeois culture beneath the protagonist’s punky youth, “Ripcord” contends with it. All the narrator’s capacity for deflection comes into play as he deals with the humdrum present, the reality that nothing will change—certainly not himself.

Lippens picks the right subject to explore this midlife immovability: sex. For his narrator, promiscuity is a respite and a diversion, never a tool to open possibilities for the future, not even when he gets close to someone who makes him briefly engage in “romantic delusions.” This lover, Dustin, is younger and married. He misses the narrator’s conversational reference to the actor Angie Dickinson and dislikes one of his favorite novels because it lacks “redemption.” Yet they have a dynamic that tempts the narrator to lower his defenses, until Dustin breaks things off because his husband reads their texts.

The protagonist reacts to the fissure with a self-lacerating wit that can’t hide an underlying egotism. “I am a cliché. An older man having a nonaffair with a younger man. A lonely man in a lousy room saying tired words,” he disparages himself. His pride may be bruised, but, even during a vulnerable moment, it offers a kind of fortitude. Describing his abjection fuels his sense of superiority over others and his own circumstances. “They don’t understand when I say I’m a piece of shit, I mean they are pieces of shit too,” he says of acquaintances who fail to appreciate his self-effacing humor. “I’m using myself as the stool sample for humanity.”

Lippens’s punch lines are unstoppable, his narrators like a tawdry standup comedian going whole hog in an empty theatre. “Bastards” is a meditation on performance as the self-aware heart of the gay working class. The book begins with the narrator, who has recently emerged from a psychiatric hold, rhinestoning the dress of a drag-queen friend—named Grace Period—in the middle of the night. This, he informs us, is his own grace period from the various types of social performance that subsistence demands of him: “The hours between midnight and dawn are best because I don’t have to stay in character.”

To lose character means, among other things, to let his stiff upper lip loosen, to grow morose about ghosts. “Bastards” perseverates over one friend in particular, Rudy, an older gay man with an acidic outlook to match the narrator’s own. Recollections of Rudy reappear throughout, accompanied by a simultaneous thrill and annoyance with his rambling opinions—Rudy, too, could banter like there was always a camera on him. His prickliness molded the narrator, who was a teen-ager when they met. “Rudy was first chair in the mental peanut gallery of faces I pictured observing my life. I measured my actions in his imagined reactions. I saw the world in particular lights—Rudy-worthy details popped—so I could report back to him, a double agent.”

Both men “understood the obituarist’s tally and the gossip’s snark,” a useful dichotomy for Lippens’s trilogy. If “My Dead Book” is a collective eulogy and “Ripcord” a sardonic pillow book, “Bastards” merges these forms, spangling self-mockery across its surface as a survival mechanism and a means of fabricating delight.

Lippens’s characters bear an outspoken contempt for so many aspects of contemporary gay life—the drag-brunch fad, for instance, which the aforementioned Grace Period regards as inferior to the plucky drag scene of the eighties or nineties. Their disdain, though, is bespoke and self-protective, fanged yet functionally harmless. These are outsiders asserting the validity of a history that is always being forgotten.

In spite of their occasional snobbishness, they refuse America’s truly destructive snobberies—the supreme regard accorded to money and material success, coupledom (rather than singledom), owning property (instead of renting it)—and lay bare how these values can feel inescapable even within oppressed microcosms like the queer community. The trilogy rebuffs the primacy of coastal metropolises and prestigious jobs, the sort of hierarchies the narrator of “Bastards” scorns as “status fetishes.” Lippens denies the premium that gay-male culture places on youth and masculinity. After an encounter with a man who insults him for not being butch enough, the narrator of “Ripcord” goes back on the app where they met: “I changed my profile to: 5”7’ fem with the face of an embittered sea captain, the voice of a pissed off fey concierge, and a body like an unmade bed.” The narrator of “Bastards” rues to a pal at a catering gig, “Last few years my close friends have winnowed to other effeminate gay men our age.” He doesn’t resent his friends or the intimacy of his circle, but he begrudges the normativity that has all but forced him into a narrow milieu.

The issue, “Bastards” indicates, is one of class. The prejudices of a superficial society obsessed with social position nag at these books. Lippens is too much an aesthete, too slyly capable with surfaces, to ever use the term “classism.” His trilogy is a diagnosis dressed up in a rhinestone gown, shining brightly before a trick of the light reveals the rot underneath. ♦

title: Defending the Midterms from Donald Trump
author: @NewYorker
content:
The reporter Barton Gellman discusses threats to the upcoming elections.

October 30, 2026

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up for our daily newsletter to get the best of The New Yorker in your inbox.

Amid all the prognostication about which party will emerge triumphant during the midterms, there has also been increasing alarm: Will it be a free and fair election? As soon as Donald Trump returned to office, he began making moves to create disruption—demanding private voter data from states, threatening election officials with jail time, and even seizing ballots from prior elections to investigate alleged fraud. And although, so far, none of the White House’s efforts have threatened to significantly alter the results, the Department of Justice has hinted that there is more to come. The U.S. Attorney General, Todd Blanche, has not ruled out using the force of law to prevent election certifications. Furthermore, a lawsuit from the Trump Administration against the State of Alaska is already under way, before a single vote has even been counted. The reporter Barton Gellman and David Remnick discuss the threats to the midterm elections and Gellman’s new piece, “The State Officials Defending the Midterms from the President.”

Further reading:

  • “How ICE Is Targeting the 2026 Midterms,” by Jonathan Blitzer
  • “What the Gerrymandering Wars Mean for the Midterms—and 2028,” by Isaac Chotiner
  • “The G.O.P.’s Latest Voter-Suppression Plan,” by Sue Halpern
  • “Donald Trump Already Knows the 2026 Election Is ‘Rigged,’ ” by Susan B. Glasser
