title: Obama’s Great Skewering of Trump
author: @NewYorker
content:
Leave it to Barack Obama to deliver the Democratic line of the midterms, a brilliant if slightly obscure riff on Donald Trump’s home-renovation obsession at a time when Americans wish he would spend more time on the price of groceries than on the amount of gold in the Oval Office. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” the former President joked during a rally over the weekend in newly competitive Ohio, where his party is hoping, five days from now, to win both the governorship and a U.S. Senate seat just two years after losing the state to Trump by more than eleven points. After Trump and his allies spent days complaining about this supposedly élitist slur against one of Middle America’s favorite restaurant chains, Obama came back with what was arguably an even sharper disquisition on his successor’s misplaced priorities.

“I’m not making this up. He, the President of the United States, is spending time supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office,” Obama said at another rally on Wednesday, this time in suburban Atlanta, making an allusion to one of the more telling revelations in “Regime Change,” a recent best-selling book by the Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. “He is literally doing arts and crafts while we are fighting a war and trying to deal with out-of-control prices.”

As for the matter of Trump, Saddam, and the Cheesecake Factory, Obama replied with a nearly five-hundred-word skewering of the “whole-of-government response” to his joke. Rather than try to paraphrase its genius, I will merely quote it at length:

That was the interesting thing about how the Administration responded to the speech I gave the other day. They did not dispute what I said about them being directly responsible for rising prices. Did not argue with that! They did not deny tariffs were contributing to higher costs for families. They didn’t say anything about that! I accused this Administration based on the facts that they were engaging in unprecedented levels of corruption. They didn’t say anything about that! The President wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison. That part didn’t bother him! But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comments. He took great umbrage. He said I didn’t understand the work of the artisans in the White House.

And they mobilized. I mean, it’s all crazy, but this was the really crazy part. They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke—not to inflation but to that joke! The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy, the person who’s supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable, the guy who’s supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation and reduce interest rates. They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory. . . . And the Treasury Secretary, he happens to be a former hedge-fund manager worth half a billion dollars. And he was out there in front of the Cheesecake Factory, explaining how he ordered the delicious French-dip cheeseburger instead of the egg rolls. Now, look, this is not something I ever thought of. I inherited this major financial crisis. I never called my Treasury Secretary, Tim Geithner, and said, ‘Man, you’ve got to go to Arby’s, order roast beef. No cheese, though. That may look élitist.’

To everybody out there, including the press, I want you to understand this. This is what I mean when I say these are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems, so they’d rather have the media and you talking about the Cheesecake Factory.

More than ten billion dollars has already been spent on campaign advertising in this election cycle, which is projected to be the most expensive in American history. But, among the multitudes, it’s hard to imagine a single TV spot as simultaneously incisive, cutting, and funny as Obama managed to be the other night with this epic retort. Obama himself stopped at least a half dozen times to laugh at his own material. And yet it was also one of the most on-message speeches I’ve heard this fall, pulling together Trump’s unpopular war in the Middle East, rising prices at home, and the entitled indifference of our callous and corrupt rulers into one long, strange story about the Cheesecake Factory. Props to a professional. That is not easy to do.

As Obama was bringing down the house in Clayton County, Georgia, it happened that Trump was taking the stage in Chillicothe, Ohio, for a rally of his own. As if to underscore the split-screen reality of these midterm elections, one of the big questions going into Trump’s appearance was whether he would, as he has done repeatedly in recent days, talk about the impressive backside of Ohio’s Republican Senate candidate, the incumbent Jon Husted. (Trump did, first admitting to “looking at his ass, and it was strong as hell,” then blaming the “fake news” for making fun of him about it.) Another unknown was whether the President would take Obama’s bait, and spend yet more time reinforcing how out of touch with the American public he is by going on and on about his White House renovations. (He did this, too, explaining for a full five minutes why he had to fix the “half-broken” and “terrible”-looking executive mansion and how Obama “doesn’t understand cleanliness, doesn’t understand broken, cracked stone and sidewalk.”)

Perhaps Trump’s signature moment came twenty minutes later, after detours to discuss those dastardly Haitian refugees in Springfield, Ohio, why Vivek Ramaswamy was right to run what is now an infamous ad quoting his opponent’s estranged mother, and how he made the Venezuelans give him a million barrels of oil a day, “free of charge.” The subject? His own cognitive abilities. Like Obama’s riff, it defies easy paraphrase. To wit:

I’m a very high-I.Q. person. Don’t forget I’m the only President to pass without exception—I passed three cognitive tests. I’m the only President that agreed to take them. And they’re hard, you know? Obama—Obama couldn’t have passed it. Biden we don’t even talk about. Republicans wouldn’t have passed them. I won’t mention names because I’m supposed to be a nice Republican. But I passed them. I got three of them all—and, by the way, you know what they do with the cognitive tests? The first one is easy. They have a lion, a bear, a snake, and a camel. They say, which one is the snake, O.K.? That’s question one.

Question two is a little bit—by the time you get up to fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, you gotta be freaking smart to answer. . . . But I passed them. So, no other Presidents agreed to take them. It’s a very powerful test, very highly respected test, very well-known test. Thirty questions, very hard, some of them. After you get to fifteen—oh, after you get to twenty, twenty-five, very few people. I’m one of the only persons. I passed it all three times. I aced it, zero mistakes, all three times. But, no, that’s—that’s the good news. So, I said to the doctor—I think one of the doctors is here tonight. They have a whole team of doctors standing there watching you. ‘Mr. President, take the number sixty-four, multiply it times seven, divide by three, add 1,019, subtract seventy-four, multiply by nine. Sir, what do you have?’ Now, I know the number to that. Does anybody else know the number to that—it is? That was as you got to the end. And that wasn’t as hard as some of them. So—anyway, so I aced it all three times. . . .

This, to be clear, is a shortened version of the President’s lecture, which omits both a long explanation of how he came to decide to take the cognitive test in the first place and a discussion of his late uncle, the physicist John Trump, who was blessed with “athletic genetics” as well as “smart genetics” and “just got named the No. 1 professor in the history of M.I.T.”

By this point in the rally, Trump had been speaking for nearly an hour, without making any effort to address the issue that is driving this election—voter discontent across the political spectrum with the high prices that he promised to bring down on Day One of his Presidency but which continue to rise owing to the war that he promised not to start. When he did mention the economy, it was all golden-age-this and I’m-so-great-that. “We are making a fortune in this country,” Trump insisted, saying it with such conviction it sounded as though he was thinking of his own ballooning bank account. On a less upbeat note, he warned that if Democrats come back to power, America will be looking at a dim future of “open borders,” “transgender for everybody,” and a “1929-style economic depression.”

Obama, as a campaigner and as a President, always excelled as a teller of hard truths. Trump, in this as in so much else, remains his inverse. If reality is a problem, he’ll just create an alternative. “Now you have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he told the cheering crowd in Ohio. The pitchman will never stop pitching.

Two Presidents, two Americas. For ten endless years, our politics has been all about the vast gap that separates these two men, and the near-impossible task of trying to understand how a country that elected Obama twice could, so soon after, do the same for Trump. Watching them both on Wednesday night, toggling between screens and alternate universes as they shot barbs at each other, was a reminder of how very long we’ve been stuck in this loop.

What’s different this time is a sense—and, until there are votes counted and races called, it’s just a sense—that real-world events have intervened to make this less of an intractably divided country and more of a place where at least some shared truths are still possible. Perhaps the biggest and most motivating truth is that prices are too damn high, which comes with the corollary that Trump has no one to blame for this but himself. Headed into the midterms, America is not a fifty-fifty nation on these questions; it is a country where sixty per cent or more of the people disapprove of the President and do not support his policies.

David Plouffe, the strategist who helped Obama win election to the White House in 2008, observed the other day that, when a big wave is building in American politics, it’s almost impossible for individual politicians to swim against it. “Voters just shut you out, and that’s what’s happening right now,” he said during an interview at The New Yorker Festival. “When you’re in a landslide scenario against you, your political money and political ads have no capability to compete with reality.”

He and other political handicappers believe that is what is happening to Trump and his Republicans right now. The idea has taken hold so firmly in Washington that much of the talk here is about the Democratic infighting that’s already broken out about how to run the Congress that everyone now assumes the Party will soon win. In the prediction markets, there’s currently a sixty-eight-per-cent chance of Democrats winning the Senate and a ninety-two-per-cent chance of Democrats winning the House.

In five days, we’ll know if the wave has in fact materialized, if voters in places such as Iowa, North Carolina, and Ohio, which went for Obama before they went for Trump, have decided that enough is enough. But on Election Night and beyond, I’ll also be thinking about what then happens to Trump and those who’ve stayed with the President in his reality-defying bubble, the folks who were cheering him in Chillicothe, and who’ve been with him the whole long, strange way. Just what is it we think will happen if and when the bubble bursts? ♦

title: How a Kansas Megachurch Pastor Might Determine Who Wins the Senate
author: @NewYorker
content:
One recent Sunday, Adam Hamilton, the Kansas pastor who has been running an unexpectedly competitive Democratic bid for U.S. senator, was scheduled to visit four churches around Kansas City. As he settled into a pew at Oak Ridge Baptist Church, he was fretting. “I want to stay for the entire worship service,” he said.

People milled around the sanctuary, greeting one another warmly. Nearly everyone there was Black; all the churches in the day’s lineup were Missionary Baptist, a historically Black denomination. Hamilton, wearing a neatly ironed blue suit and carrying his personal Bible, greeted parishioners warmly, as he has done nearly every Sunday morning of his adult life. Finally, Ricky Turner, the church’s pastor, called him up to stand by the podium. “Adam knows that we don’t give the mike to politicians,” Turner said. But Hamilton was not just any politician, he said: “This is a man of God.” When Turner’s daughter was in a car accident recently, “I got a call from Adam Hamilton,” he said. “You know what he did? He just started praying for me.” The congregation cheered.

Much has been made of the fact that Democrats are running avowedly Christian candidates in November’s midterms. There’s James Talarico, the Presbyterian seminarian running for the U.S. Senate in Texas, who has got in trouble for such theological provocations as “God is nonbinary.” Or Rob Sand, the Iowa gubernatorial candidate, who likes to say that “Jesus is for the little guy.” But no other candidate is as well established in the Christian world as Hamilton. He is the founding pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, which, with twenty-three thousand members across nine locations, is the country’s largest United Methodist congregation. His books and Bible studies are read all over the country.

Less than a minute after Turner finished speaking, Hamilton was out the door, moving so fast that a normal person would have to jog to keep up. After a twenty-minute drive, he strode into Forest Grove Baptist Church, where about forty people were at the morning worship service. Here, Hamilton got to take the pulpit. “My deepest desire is to help people know Christ,” he said. As he’d watched the news in the past year and a half, he said, he’d thought, “This does not look like the kingdom of God I have prayed for and preached for my entire life.” During Lent, he and his wife fasted every day, and they decided that he should jump into the race after Easter. “I’m going to ask you not for your vote—I’m going to ask for your prayers,” he said. “That God will continue to guide me, strengthen me, and help me—and, if I do get elected on November 3rd, that God would use me to push back the darkness in our country.”

Polling suggests that Hamilton may just win. President Donald Trump’s policies have been hard on Kansas. Diesel prices are sky-high. Lower tariffs on beef have hurt cattle ranchers. ICE recently raided meat-processing plants in several cities in rural southwestern Kansas. Trump even threatened to ban jets made by Bombardier, a Canadian company; the company’s American headquarters are in Wichita.

Roger Marshall, the incumbent Republican senator, has backed Trump on almost all these policies. He has also developed a rough reputation of his own. This fall, the Times published an investigation showing that Marshall, a retired ob-gyn, had sued more than seven hundred patients for missing payments; eighty-one were arrested. At the Kansas State Fair in September, Marshall protested that he had a business to run: “We had three hundred employees.” The audience booed.

Kansas is a red state, where a plurality of voters are registered Republicans, but it has an independent streak. In 2022, after the fall of Roe v. Wade, it was one of the first states to consider a referendum that would have led to an abortion ban; the measure failed. The governor, Laura Kelly, is a Democrat; another Democrat, Kathleen Sebelius, served as governor from 2003 to 2009 and has won four statewide races. She thinks that her success can be replicated this year. This is “the first time in my life that I have seen people being able to connect the dots very clearly,” she told me. “It is people understanding: the President launched a war in Iran, and my gas is unaffordable.” Bob Beatty, a political-science professor at Washburn University in Topeka, told me, “For a Democrat to win statewide, they need to win in northeast Kansas—which is Johnson County especially—by twenty-plus points, and then not get slaughtered in western Kansas.” Johnson County, south of Kansas City, is where twenty-three per cent of the state’s registered voters live. It’s also where COR is situated.

Especially after the bruising 2024 election, Democrats desperately want to win in red states. Hamilton is like an unexpected miracle: he entered late and mounted a surprisingly strong campaign. Improbably, whoever wins this seat may end up determining which party controls the Senate. Still, candidates like Hamilton are an uncomfortable fit for the Democratic Party. And, perhaps just as important, the Democratic Party may be an uncomfortable fit for Hamilton’s church.

Hamilton grew up in the southern suburbs of Kansas City, without much religious instruction. When he was a teen-ager, a street preacher convinced him to visit a Pentecostal church, and he started attending regularly. At fourteen, he asked to give his life to Jesus. After high school, he married a girl he had met at church, and then began his studies at Oral Roberts University, a well-known Pentecostal college. But Hamilton craved a broader intellectual tradition for his faith. He eventually discovered the eighteenth-century theologian John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, who promoted a combination of social activism and personal piety.

After seminary, Hamilton began building a church, holding the first services in the chapel of a funeral home in 1990. To increase attendance, he sent postcards to every address in the surrounding city of Leawood, Kansas. When someone new came, he would stop by their house the next day to give them a coffee mug, a process that later became known internally as “mugging.” By the early two-thousands, the congregation was well into the thousands. Hamilton usually preaches forty Sundays a year, with his sermons beamed into other locations on huge video screens.

The United Methodist Church has historically held together a wide theological spectrum. “Methodists are chameleons,” Mark Holland, a pastor who served as mayor of Kansas City, Kansas, told me. “In the Northeast, we look a lot like the Unitarians. In the South, we look a lot like the Southern Baptists.” Several people told me that Hamilton is from the more evangelical side of that spectrum. It’s a fraught description: the term has become associated, at least in some people’s minds, more with a political identity than with a religious one. On our way out of Oak Ridge, Pastor Turner said that his parishioners should want to put Christians in office, and “not just evangelicals!”

As I hurried after Hamilton, he agreed to the term, but with caveats. “ ‘Evangel’ means good news,” he told me. “I’ve always considered myself what I would call a progressive evangelical, and that is somebody who cares deeply about people coming to faith in Christ, experiencing what Jesus talked about—the new birth—being filled with the Holy Spirit, and then being committed to love their neighbors as they love themselves.”

Democrats are often willing to go along with sentiments like “love your neighbor.” Even progressive crusaders like Elizabeth Warren pepper their speeches with references to “the least of these,” from Matthew 25, or the parable of Jesus flipping the money changers’ tables, from Matthew 21. But anything more Jesus-y than that is uncommon. “I’ve been here for a while, in Congress,” Emanuel Cleaver, a U.S. congressman from Kansas City, Missouri, who is also a Methodist pastor, told me. “One of the things that I learned early on was that Democrats have a nervousness around their love for Jesus.” (Hamilton’s campaign declined to make time for the candidate to speak about his faith ahead of the election.)

There’s been an interesting religious dynamic this midterm cycle. Michael Wear, a former Obama Administration official who runs the Center for Christianity and Public Life, told me, “Hamilton, Talarico, and so many of these candidates who are leading with their faith have had to spend a lot of time on the campaign trail, and a lot of money, making clear that they are not one of those Christians.”

After Hamilton got done church-hopping, volunteers held a get-out-the-vote event at a brewery not far from COR. At the bar, a group of forty-something regulars were posted up watching the Chiefs game; they hadn’t come for the Hamilton event, but it was a conversation piece. “I one hundred and ten per cent recognize the hesitation of electing a pastor, because of the Christian nationalism being put forward by the right wing,” a woman named Julia said. She had cast an early ballot for Hamilton, but the pastor part of him gave her pause. “I am concerned about the infiltration of religion into politics in any capacity,” she said.

On the campaign trail, Hamilton loves to talk up the political diversity of his church: according to COR’s internal numbers, it’s about forty per cent Republicans and forty per cent Democrats, with most of the rest being Independents. He has leaned into the story of his own independence, noting that he only recently switched his voter registration to Democrat. This is a little misleading. Hamilton preached at a prayer service following Obama’s second Inauguration; he also served on the President’s Advisory Council on Faith-based and Neighborhood Partnerships.

Hamilton pitches his church as a place for thinking people. Shere-Ling Kraus-Yao, a church member who attended the get-out-the-vote event, told me that she likes that you “don’t check your brain at the door when you come in.” It is central to Hamilton’s identity that COR is a place where people can disagree well about hard things. This attitude is not necessarily in vogue in contemporary politics. “After President Obama, the Democratic Party—like the Republican Party—grew much more ideologically exclusive,” Joel Hunter, the former pastor of a Florida megachurch called Northland Church, who served as an adviser to Obama, said. “Neither one of them was trending toward a big-tent standard.”

Take Hamilton’s writing on abortion. In his book “Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White,” he writes that abortion needs to be safe and available. But, he continues, “I believe conception is a miraculous event in which we have become co-creators with God, and is to be violated only under the most extreme of situations.” He favors the morning-after pill, which works for up to three days after unprotected sex, over surgical abortion. And, he says, “the church must, with compassion and love, articulate to its members the reasons they should choose to carry a child to term when the pregnancy is unplanned.” It’s rare these days to hear elected Democrats at any level expressing this kind of view.

Yet Hamilton’s opponents have cast him as “too liberal for Kansas.” They have attacked him for his “inclusivist” approach to salvation, which suggests that God may still save people who don’t explicitly recognize Jesus as the Son of God; Senator Ted Cruz called this “heretical.” Hamilton once noted in a sermon that cattle ranching exacerbates climate change. This was turned into a line about how he wants people to repent for eating beef; Hamilton ran an ad in which he tucks into a steak. More seriously, the Marshall campaign has focussed on a situation from two decades ago in which two boys who participated in a COR retreat alleged that they had been sexually assaulted by an adult volunteer. The church investigated, but did not immediately contact the authorities, which Hamilton now says he should have done.

Republicans have also tried to associate Hamilton with transgender activism; during a rally in Wichita, Trump claimed that he believes in “making children transgender.” But Hamilton has expressed fairly conservative views on this issue. “There are two genders, male and female,” he said during a debate in October. “I have a twelve-year-old granddaughter. I don’t want biological men or boys competing against her.” Hamilton is now fully affirming of same-sex marriages, but it took him a while to get there: in 2004, after a sermon during which he said that “I don’t know” the right answer on this issue, more than a thousand people left his church, most of whom felt that he had capitulated on a core Biblical teaching.

In recent years, the United Methodist Church has faced tremendous internal disagreement over L.G.B.T.Q. issues; those debates, which culminated in a 2024 decision to ordain gay clergy and to effectively allow same-sex marriages, led to more than eight thousand churches leaving the denomination. This ordeal has become another Republican attack line. “Was he leading from the middle when one out of four churches left his denomination?” Marshall said during October’s debate.

It’s a little surreal to see complex denominational battles become fodder for campaign ads. Hamilton does have significant influence within the U.M.C., but he has generally used it to ease factional differences. “All through these debates around human sexuality and the potential splits in the United Methodist Church, he’s always tried to have broad shoulders to hold the center together,” Brett Opalinski, a Methodist pastor and a professor at Emory, told me.

For others who followed the U.M.C. drama closely, though, Hamilton’s actions made him seem less trustworthy—as though he were willing to bend on core theological principles. Many of the churches that left the U.M.C. describe themselves as “traditionalists”: they believe that a faithful reading of the Bible does not support same-sex marriage. Brad Kirk, a Methodist pastor in the rural town of Kingman, Kansas, was once part of a young pastors’ network that Hamilton ran. His church left the U.M.C. several years ago, and he now knows a number of people who feel that they can’t vote for Hamilton because of his approach to Scripture. “The whole idea of electing someone who will represent a group of people is that they will stand firm,” Kirk told me, emphasizing that he was speaking for himself, not his church. “It’s that accommodation that bothers me most.”

Thirty-six years ago, Linda MacRoberts got a postcard about the Church of the Resurrection’s first Christmas Eve service, and she decided to go. She was taken by Hamilton’s message, and became one of COR’s founding members. “He is, in the very best sense, a true believer,” she told me. But when she heard that he was running for Senate, “I was very ambivalent about it. I thought he’d be swimming with sharks,” she said. She doesn’t like that his campaign has run ads about political scandals “like Jeffrey Epstein, and they’re showing this dark picture of Roger Marshall.”

Before Hamilton entered the Senate race, he was planning to retire from COR in 2030. His run has left the church trying to navigate its new political role. During the Chiefs game, a hundred or so people gathered at the church’s main location, in Leawood, for 5 P.M. worship. “You might be wondering, ‘Where is everybody else tonight?’ ” Joshua Clough, an associate pastor, said. “You are the true faithful,” he joked. “Your spot is deserved in Heaven.” A stained-glass Jesus loomed over everything.

Afterward, Clough told me that the church has “tried really hard to separate the political campaign from the work that the church has always done.” It’s been frustrating for staff to see Hamilton’s careful, nuanced approach get pilloried as the agenda of “a radical-left lunatic,” which is what the President recently called him during the rally in Wichita. “Our posture isn’t to defend everything but to live our values out through serving others,” Clough said. He sees the campaign as an opportunity, he added. “We get to share a different narrative about Christian faith that most never hear.” ♦

title: “Wild Horse Nine” Gets Lost on Easter Island
author: @NewYorker
content:
The first time John Malkovich played a killer trained by the C.I.A., he was a man of many disguises, elusive and unpredictable as the wind. The film was “In the Line of Fire” (1993), and his character, nicknamed Booth, was a psychotically disgruntled agency alum, plotting to murder the President with a custom-built plastic gun and a bullet that he stored in a rabbit’s foot. His other weapon was his voice, at once coldly precise and dangerously soft; never before had Malkovich’s distinctly odd cadences sounded so menacing. Booth spent a lot of time on the phone, taunting a veteran Secret Service agent (Clint Eastwood) about his failure, decades earlier, to protect John F. Kennedy. “Late at night, when the demons come, do you see the rifle coming out of that window?” he drawled. “Or do you see Kennedy’s head being blown apart?”

That tragedy looms heavily, but also with an air of jokey inconsequence, over “Wild Horse Nine,” a new film written and directed by Martin McDonagh. It begins in 1973, in Santiago, Chile, where Chris Carlisle (Malkovich), a longtime C.I.A. operative, is stationed. Early on, he reminisces about the popularly elected regimes that he’s toppled, from Guatemala to Congo, and—here his voice drops to a low murmur—acknowledges a prominent role in the Kennedy assassination. Yet, despite this dabbling in POTUS-cide, Chris is something of an anti-Booth; he has too much debonair wit, too much bon-vivant style. He and his loyal protégé, Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell), are headed to Easter Island for a week, and Chris, looking dandy in bright-colored neckties and a porkpie hat, has no use for disguises. As for a rabbit’s foot, forget it: Chris’s luck has run out. He’s dying of cancer and has decided that Easter Island will be his last hurrah. He wants Lee, whose marksmanship he trusts as much as his friendship, to hasten his departure.

Lee, whose frequent exasperation with Chris is a sure sign of love, has his own problems back home in the U.S., chiefly a “drunk wife who fucks clowns.” That’s Chris’s odd, harsh appraisal, and it is repeated, mirthlessly, when we finally meet said wife (Parker Posey), badgering Lee over the phone. Whenever McDonagh hits a stale comic patch like this, he retreats swiftly into the trappings of plot: Lee is understandably less than thrilled about Chris’s instant-death wish, but, by all appearances, M.J. (a cranky Steve Buscemi), the C.I.A.’s South American bureau chief, already has a finger on the trigger. Chris, often strung out on morphine, his memory and his wits addled by cancer, has become a jaw-flapping liability.

Despite the far-flung setting and the spy-thriller machinations, then, we are in terrain that McDonagh knows all too well: the bloody buddy comedy. Like his film “In Bruges” (2008), “Wild Horse Nine” follows two hit men on holiday, and, like “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), it conjures the verdant magic of a remote island setting. Yet the flavor of the proceedings is markedly different. In “Inisherin,” a bitter clash between two friends, played by Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson (who both also starred in “In Bruges”), felt exquisitely of a piece with the local elements: the mists, the jagged rocks, the salty tang of the sea. The outdoors lent a wry, soulful grandeur to the characters’ expletive-riddled bickering.

There are profanities aplenty in “Wild Horse Nine,” as there are in all McDonagh’s movies and plays. (Cut out the F-bombs and most of them would run barely an hour.) And the vast expanse of Easter Island, majestically filmed by the cinematographer Ben Davis, is astonishing to behold. (Lee himself can’t resist filming with a Super 8 camera, and his grainy images add welcome blips of texture.) Feral horses roam the landscape, and they give the movie both its title and its desired genre: McDonagh strives for the laconic sweep of a classic Western. But not all material can command a space this vast, and I suspect that John Ford himself might have struggled to wring much poetry from Chris and Lee, two ugly-American blowhards wisecracking their way around paradise. Really, the shenanigans could have been transplanted anywhere: picture two guys farting at Stonehenge for an hour or two, only to realize, like the ancients before them, that it makes an awfully nice burial ground.

Within such comedic confines, and with a surprising dearth of violent mayhem, “Wild Horse Nine” strains for thematic expansiveness. Ostensibly, the film is about the mixed blessings of friendship, the soul-corroding nature of violence, the horrors of U.S. foreign policy, the possibility of redemption, and the inescapability of death. But it’s the stiffest, least cohesive film on those subjects you could imagine. McDonagh organizes his scenes into thematic blocks, and whenever he loses interest in one block he simply switches, mechanically, to the next. The conversations that he’s written for Chris and Lee toggle between humor and pathos, between self-satisfied snark and self-conscious elegy, and there’s barely a moment when you don’t hear the grinding of tonal gears. (You hear it in the music, too; the Rolling Stones’ “Out of Time” isn’t the subtlest of needle drops.)

McDonagh’s dialogue is famed for its staccato crackle, but here he slows the characters’ rhythms, as if to accommodate the diminution of Chris’s body and mind, and packs dead air around everyone’s lines. Yet within those rhythms Malkovich does locate odd, narcotized flashes of poetry. His voice is lower and shakier than usual, and the gleam in his eyes sometimes goes ambiguously dull: are Chris’s mental lapses real, or part of some long con? Chris hasn’t lost his saucy erudition; one of his funnier bits is a mid-breakfast monologue on why “gay countries,” like France, produce the highest-quality cheeses. But he seems on precarious ground, no longer certain of his punch lines. He is also rediscovering the guilt and terror of his Catholic upbringing, and he wonders if, after a life spent overthrowing democracies—the coup that will depose President Salvador Allende is in the offing—he has a chance in hell of entering Heaven.

Easter Island is, of course, dotted with towering volcanic-stone figures with large, elongated faces. Chris and Lee refer to them as “the big heads,” and when a tourist couple gently note that the Indigenous term is “moai,” Lee erupts in fury—though Rockwell, who’s good at modulating an explosion, makes clear that Lee is exaggerating his rage for Chris’s benefit. Earlier, at the Santiago airport, they had an awkward run-in with two Chilean college students, Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) and Alicia (Ailín Salas), one of whom explained that the Indigenous name for Easter Island is Rapa Nui. “You shouldn’t even know the word ‘Indigenous’ at your age,” Chris replied.

It’s telling that McDonagh hammers the word “Indigenous” repeatedly and contemptuously—as opposed to, say, “local” or “Polynesian.” Back in the seventies, the term was less prevalent in English than it is today, but McDonagh, not for the first time, is eager to mock the language of the contemporary liberal scold. Farrell’s “In Bruges” character wasted no opportunity to call a dwarf a midget; in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” (2017), McDonagh’s most pugnacious and polarizing work, Rockwell played a racist cop, annoyed that “persons of color” had replaced his favorite epithet. You could argue, I suppose, that a film shouldn’t be reduced to its characters’ politics. But, by now, it’s hard to assume that these smug linguistic sensitivities—wielded only, of course, in response to other people’s smug linguistic sensitivities—belong to anyone other than McDonagh himself. And they speak to the narrow view that he takes of his chosen setting and the harrowing historical episode into which he’s seen fit to shoehorn his characters.

“Three Billboards” hinged on the racist cop’s reformation, and “Wild Horse Nine,” with less outrageousness and more finesse, undertakes its own dubiously reconstructive exercise. Despite its misanthropic pose, the film wants very badly for us to like and even love Chris, to find him as charming as he is cancel-worthy. Chris regards his role in the deaths and disappearances of thousands of innocents with a weary shrug—and, on rare dark nights of the soul, a piddling note of regret. At one point, he notes his incongruous fondness for the local insects. “Sometimes I feel like I care more about the moths of Chile,” he says, “than I do about the people of Chile.”

McDonagh grants us a touristic view of Chile masquerading as a geopolitical one, and his dramatic aims are as obvious and limited as his emotional agenda. We’re meant to find Chris pitiable because of his diagnosis, and we’re meant to find him redeemable when he offers sincere advice to the naïvely idealistic Monica, warning her of the forthcoming horrors of the Pinochet regime. The final passages of “Wild Horse Nine” are at once swift and interminable, the action-thriller elements snapping into place at last, only to be hijacked by an exceedingly long goodbye. You can’t accuse McDonagh of not knowing his priorities; we are to shed bountiful tears for Chris, with perhaps a few to spare for his collateral damage. Some of us may be forgiven for resisting the invitation. I remained dry of eye—and rooted for the cancer. ♦
